# Instructions

Given an input text output it transposed.

Roughly explained, the transpose of a matrix:

```text
ABC
DEF
```

is given by:

```text
AD
BE
CF
```

Rows become columns and columns become rows.
See [transpose][].

If the input has rows of different lengths, this is to be solved as follows:

- Pad to the left with spaces.
- Don't pad to the right.

Therefore, transposing this matrix:

```text
ABC
DE
```

results in:

```text
AD
BE
C
```

And transposing:

```text
AB
DEF
```

results in:

```text
AD
BE
 F
```

In general, all characters from the input should also be present in the transposed output.
That means that if a column in the input text contains only spaces on its bottom-most row(s), the corresponding output row should contain the spaces in its right-most column(s).

[transpose]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transpose

Use the instructions above to complete `transpose.py`. Keep the existing function and class names: tests you cannot see import them. Use only the Python standard library.

text:
I've written `transpose` in `transpose.py`, and it gives the right output for the examples in the instructions plus a few edge cases I tried.

**How it works:** it splits the input into rows. Each row is padded on the right with spaces up to the length of the longest row at or below it. The columns are then read off as the new rows. This puts the padding on the left in the output and never adds any on the right. Any trailing spaces that were in the original input are kept.

**What I checked:** the project has no test files, so I ran the function on a few inputs by hand:
- `"ABC\nDE"` gives `"AD\nBE\nC"`.
- `"AB\nDEF"` gives `"AD\nBE\n F"`.
- An empty string gives an empty string.
- A triangle of rows getting longer and a set of uneven sentence lines also came out as expected.

The function name is unchanged, and it uses only the standard library.
